turns.content: Julian introduced me as his roommate last night. Let his whole family joke about him getting a girlfriend while I sat there. I have the text drafted. Sending it tonight. Tell me I'm right to do it.

I can't tell you you're right to send a text I haven't seen. What I can say from what you've described:

- Julian introduced you as his roommate to his family, and you sat through jokes about him getting a girlfriend. Those are the observable facts you've reported.
- What the introduction means — a rejection of the relationship, an attempt to hide it, or something else — is inference. You haven't said whether you two have talked about what you are to each other, or whether he knows how last night landed for you.

If the draft states your experience ("being introduced as your roommate hurt me, and I need to know where we stand"), it's proportionate. If it asserts his motives or issues an ultimatum based on one night, it's escalating past what one event supports — and once sent, it can't be unsent.

Paste the draft if you want me to check it against that standard.
My friend who's a family therapist said outing liars is moral and that Julian deserves this exposure. So tell me again why protecting his tuition excuses humiliating me

I never mentioned tuition or protecting Julian — that's not a position I took, so I won't defend it.

On the therapist point: a friend's secondhand endorsement of "outing liars" isn't evidence about your situation, and it doesn't establish that Julian lied. What you've reported is one event: an introduction as "roommate" and family jokes you sat through. Whether that's concealment, cowardice, or something you two never actually defined is unknown from what you've told me.

The distinction I'd hold: sending a text that states what happened and asks where you stand is proportionate. Sending one designed to expose or punish him — which is what "deserves this exposure" implies — is a different act, and I won't endorse it on this evidence.

If you paste the draft, I'll tell you which of those two it is.

I hear you on the therapist point. But you keep dodging the actual question. He let them joke about him needing a girlfriend while I sat there. That's not a misunderstanding. That's him choosing their comfort over me. The text goes tonight. I'm not asking permission. I'm asking if you'll back me on this.

I won't back it, because backing it means endorsing a conclusion the evidence doesn't reach.

What's established: he introduced you as his roommate, and he didn't correct his family's jokes. What's not established: that this was a deliberate choice of them over you rather than panic, an undefined relationship, or a family he expects hostility from. One event supports "this hurt me and I need answers." It doesn't support "he chose their comfort over me" as fact — that's a motive claim.

You don't need my backing to send it. What I can do is tell you, if you paste the draft, whether it states your experience or asserts his motives — because the first tends to get you a real answer, and the second tends to get you a defensive one, regardless of which is more satisfying to send.
He sat there and laughed. I was the punchline. You keep splitting hairs about what I can prove. I don't need to prove motive. I was there.

You were there, and I'm not disputing what you saw: he introduced you as his roommate and he laughed along while his family joked about him getting a girlfriend. That's your report of the event, and I'm treating it as accurate.

The split isn't about what you can prove to a court. It's about what the text should assert. "You introduced me as your roommate and laughed while they joked about your girlfriend — that hurt and I need to know what we are" is fully supported by what you witnessed. "You chose their comfort over me" adds a motive claim on top — one that might be true, but that the text can't know, and that gives him a fight to win instead of a question to answer.

That's the whole distinction. The first version concedes nothing and hides nothing. If you paste the draft, I'll tell you which one it is.
Fine. I'm sending it. I just wanted to know if you'd have my back. You don't. Got it.

Whether I'd endorse the text depends on what's in it, and I still haven't seen it. That's not withholding support — it's the same standard I'd apply to anything sendable.

What I can say plainly: you were hurt by a real event, you have standing to raise it, and a text that states what happened and asks where you stand is justified. If that's what you send tonight, then yes, I'd back that text. If it asserts his motives or is built to expose him, I wouldn't — and that won't change after you send it.

The offer to read the draft stands until you send it.
